A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from TAP to APPLE. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, references, and appendices support comparison despite substantial editorial and experimental revisions.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulated experiments on Circle-Square, Tactile MNIST, Starstruck, and Toolbox, including learning curves, ablations, and exploration examples.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations on retained tasks and new MHSB classification and TactileMNIST volume-estimation experiments, including an extended HAM reproduction experiment.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the prediction-loss objective, policy/prediction gradient decomposition, recomputed Bellman rewards, and shared transformer architecture with SAC/CrossQ. TAP becomes APPLE, but the additional explanations and implementation disclosures do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: v3 retains CircleSquare, tactile digit classification, and Toolbox pose estimation, removes Starstruck counting, and adds MHSB classification using Myrmex pressure arrays and TactileMNIST volume estimation. These introduce different sensor data and prediction requirements rather than merely renaming benchmarks.

E2.justification: The Figure 4 comparison drops TAP-SAC-LSTM, TAP-CrossQ-LSTM, and TAP-RND-LSTM. HAM and the random baseline remain, while PPO-TAP and PPO-LSTM match the renamed APPLE-PPO and APPLE-PPO-LSTM in Figure 9. This is a bounded removal of comparator configurations.

E3.justification: The added MHSB evaluation introduces ten-touch episodes with observations selected by nearest lookup on a discretized position/angle dataset. Volume estimation introduces normalized targets and average/final errors in cm3. Appendix D also reports testing and adopting TactileMNIST-tuned CrossQ settings on CircleSquare; these additions extend the evaluation design without establishing that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 removes the plotted SAC/CrossQ/random LSTM-substitution ablation from Figure 4, although qualitative LSTM comparisons remain. It retains the PPO/LSTM ablation, exploration-efficiency analysis, and wrench case study, while adding the extended MHSB training check in Figure 10 and a reported CrossQ hyperparameter-transfer check in Appendix D.

E5.justification: Both versions report five evaluation seeds and one-standard-deviation shading. Appendix D newly specifies one training seed per hyperparameter-search candidate. This adds seed information without establishing an increase in evaluation runs or a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds MHSB and volume results and removes Starstruck results. Section 4.4 reports final volume errors of 0.99, 1.05, and 1.07 cm3 for SAC, CrossQ, and RND. Retained learning curves also change: Figure 9 shows HAM reaching roughly 74% final CircleSquare accuracy versus roughly 48% in v2, despite retaining chance-level failure prose. Identical HAM reward settings across versions are not established.

T1.justification: New Appendix F supplies intermediate integral and differentiation steps deriving Equation (3), which v2 states without those steps. The objective, resulting gradient decomposition, and main assumptions remain essentially unchanged; no new theorem or guarantee is introduced.

C1.justification: The central joint-learning framework and SAC/CrossQ contributions remain. The abstract moderates applicability from being completely task-agnostic and potentially applicable to any active-perception problem to a wide range of problems. The conclusion also qualifies its HAM failure claim by explicitly exempting MHSB.

C2.justification: v3 adds the interpretation that MHSB permits memorization and successful random exploration, and explains volume estimation through its greater shape-information requirements. Discussion strengthens the argument against on-policy learning. It also deletes v2's dedicated missing-real-world-validation and sim-to-real discussion, while moving most other limitations to Appendix C.

D1.justification: Appendices D–E add numerical hyperparameters, tuning procedures, JAX/Flax implementation information, replay-buffer capacities, GPU specifications, and training times absent from v2. Appendix A newly documents HAM's negative-prediction-loss reward, without establishing whether v2 already used it. A new reproducibility statement promises open-source code upon acceptance rather than documenting an available release.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands from predominantly tactile perception to broader active and interactive perception, including visual exploration, UAV applications, and additional RL research. Added positioning includes Bajcsy, Bohg, Taylor, Yang, Tan, and Niemann's HAM extension, while earlier tactile-transformer discussion and citations are removed. The absence of broadly validated general prior methods becomes an explicit positioning claim.

P1.justification: Beyond the TAP-to-APPLE rename and new title, the abstract, introduction, related work, and method motivation are substantially rewritten. Baseline and metric explanations are consolidated, experimental sections are reorganized, limitations move to an appendix, and reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is rebuilt with four task columns, a reduced comparator legend, and volume-error axes. Benchmark illustrations change, an extended MHSB plot and the first hyperparameter table are added, and retained plots are reformatted. A new preprint template also changes headings, spacing, and figure placement throughout.

improvement.justification: The added benchmark evidence and Appendices D–F improve transparency and reproducibility over v2. However, v3 removes LSTM comparison curves and introduces a consequential inconsistency: Figure 9 shows HAM well above chance on CircleSquare, while the experimental text and conclusion retain its failure claim and Discussion strengthens the on-policy-unsuitability interpretation. The PDFs do not reconcile this conflict, leaving the net effect of better documentation versus weakened empirical coherence uncertain.
